It warns the Makkans, affirms divine decree and accountability, and promises the righteous gardens.

The surah recounts the favors of the Most Compassionate to humans and jinn: the Qur'an, creation, the order of the cosmos, and justice. It reminds them that all will perish, describes the Judgment and the fate of the wicked, then the gardens promised to the God-fearing, with the refrain: "Which of your Lord's favors will you deny?"

This surah describes the upheavals of the Day of Judgment and the sorting of people into three groups: the foremost, the people of the right, and the people of the left, each with its own destiny. It cites creation, crops, water and fire as signs of resurrection, affirms the Qur'an's divine origin, and evokes the moment of death.

The surah opens with creation glorifying Allah and a description of His attributes, then urges believers to have faith and spend in His cause before the Day when light separates them from the hypocrites. It describes the fleeting nature of worldly life, calls people to race toward forgiveness, and recalls the messengers, the Scripture, the balance and iron.

The surah opens with a woman's complaint to God about her husband's pronouncement of zihar, then sets out its ruling and expiation. It addresses sinful secret talk and the etiquette of gatherings, warns against allying with hypocrites and opponents of God, and promises success to the party of Allah.

The surah recounts the expulsion of the Banū Nadīr from Madinah and sets out how gains taken without battle are shared, so wealth does not circulate only among the rich. It praises the Emigrants and the Helpers, exposes the hypocrites' lies, urges piety and self-reckoning, and closes with God's beautiful names.

The surah forbids believers from allying with those who fought and expelled them, offering Abraham and his companions as a model, while permitting kindness and justice toward peaceful non-believers. It also rules on believing women migrants, dowries and women's pledge of allegiance, revealed around the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah.

The surah urges believers to match their deeds to their words and to stand firm in united ranks in God's way. It recalls how the peoples of Moses and Jesus rejected them, Jesus' announcement of Ahmad, and God's promise to complete His light, and it calls believers to be supporters of God's cause.

The surah opens by glorifying God, then describes the Prophet's mission to teach and purify the unlettered Arabs and those who follow. It likens those who ignore the Torah to a donkey carrying books, and challenges claims of exclusive divine favor. It ends with the rules of Friday prayer and a rebuke of those who left it for trade.

This surah describes the hypocrites: they profess faith with their tongues, use oaths as a shield, refuse to seek forgiveness, and, on the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq, threaten to expel the believers from Madinah. It urges believers not to let wealth and children distract them from remembering Allah, and to give charity before death comes.

The surah opens with all creation glorifying God, affirms that the world was created with purpose and that all return to Him. It upholds the resurrection and the Day of Mutual Loss, calls for faith, obedience and trust in God amid hardship, and describes wealth and children as a trial, urging piety and generous giving.

This surah lays out the rules of divorce and the waiting period, and calls for fair treatment of divorced women in housing, maintenance and nursing. It ties these rules to God-consciousness and trust in God, promising a way out, provision and ease. It recalls the fate of rebellious towns, the Messenger who leads people to light, and God's power and all-encompassing knowledge.

The surah opens with a gentle rebuke to the Prophet for forbidding himself what God had made lawful to please his wives. It addresses the expiation of oaths, sincere repentance and protecting one's family from the Fire, then gives examples: the wives of Noah and Lot, and Pharaoh's wife and Mary.

This surah affirms God's sovereignty and power, presents life and death as a test of deeds, and points to the flawless creation of the heavens. It describes the fate of deniers in Hell, recalls God's blessings, and urges faith, trust in Him, and readiness for the Day of gathering.

The surah defends the Prophet against the charge of madness, affirms his noble character, and warns arrogant deniers. It tells of the garden owners whose orchard was destroyed for denying the poor their share, contrasts the fate of the righteous and the wicked, and urges patience, unlike the man of the whale.

This surah speaks of the inevitable Hour and recalls the destruction of peoples who denied it, such as Thamūd, ‘Ād and Pharaoh. It portrays the fate of those given their record in the right or left hand, then affirms the Qur'an as a revelation from God, not the word of a poet or soothsayer.

The surah speaks of the punishment of the Last Day, which the disbelievers mockingly demand, and urges the Prophet to be patient. It portrays the terror of that Day and the fate of the wicked, then the qualities of faithful, prayerful believers promised Paradise, and warns the scoffers.

The surah recounts Noah's call to his people, night and day, in private and in public, to worship God and seek forgiveness, promising rain and blessings and pointing to the signs of creation. Because they persisted in rejection and idol worship, they were drowned, and Noah prayed against the wrongdoers and for the believers' forgiveness.

The surah tells how a group of jinn heard the Qur'an, believed in it, and affirmed God's oneness, while noting that some jinn are righteous and others deviant. It stresses that mosques belong to God alone, that the Prophet only conveys the message, and that knowledge of the unseen is God's alone.

The surah calls the Prophet to night prayer, measured recitation of the Qur'an, devotion and trust in God, and patience with those who deny him. It warns of the Day of Judgment and recalls Pharaoh's fate, then eases the length of the night vigil and urges prayer, charity and seeking forgiveness.

Revealed early in Mecca, this surah commands the Prophet to warn, glorify his Lord, stay pure and be patient. It portrays an arrogant opponent who dismissed the Qur'an as magic, describes Hell and its guardians, recounts the dialogue between the saved and the guilty, and closes by calling the Qur'an a reminder.

The surah deals with the Day of Resurrection and answers those who deny that bones can be reassembled. It portrays the reckoning, the agony of death, and the fate of radiant and gloomy faces. It also reassures the Prophet that God will gather and explain the Qur'an, and ends with human creation as proof of resurrection.

The surah recalls how man was created, tested and guided, free to be grateful or ungrateful. It contrasts the punishment of the disbelievers with the rewards of the righteous, who feed the needy, orphans and captives for God's sake alone. It closes by urging the Prophet to be patient and devout, and affirms that no one wills except as God wills.

The surah swears by sent-forth forces that the Day of Judgment will surely come, and describes its signs: stars extinguished, the sky split open. It recalls the destruction of earlier nations and signs of God's power in creation, repeats "Woe on that Day to the deniers," and contrasts the wicked's punishment with the righteous's reward.

This Meccan surah addresses the disputed "momentous news" of the Resurrection. It points to God's signs in the earth, mountains, sleep, night, sky and rain, then describes the Day of Judgment, the punishment awaiting the transgressors, and the reward of the righteous, ending with a warning of imminent reckoning.

The surah opens with oaths by angels carrying out God's command, then describes the terror of the Last Day and the disbelievers' denial of resurrection. It recalls Moses and the tyrant Pharaoh, points to the creation of heaven and earth as proof of God's power, contrasts the fate of the rebellious and the God-fearing, and affirms that only God knows the Hour.

The surah opens by rebuking the Prophet ﷺ for turning away from a blind man who came seeking guidance while he was addressing Makkah's leaders, then affirms that the Qur'an is an honored reminder. It recalls human creation and God's provision, and ends with Judgment Day, when faces will be bright or darkened.

The surah portrays the upheaval of the universe on the Day of Judgement: the buried baby girl is asked for what crime she was killed, records are opened, and every soul will know what it has brought. It then affirms that the Qur'an was conveyed by Gabriel, that the Prophet is not mad, and that it is a reminder to all.

The surah describes the upheaval of the heavens and the earth on the Day of Judgment, then rebukes humankind for neglecting the Generous Lord who fashioned them. It recalls the honorable angels who record every deed, the fates of the righteous and the wicked, and the Day when no soul can help another.

The surah warns those who cheat in weights and measures, reminding them of the Day when people stand before the Lord of the worlds. It contrasts the fate of the wicked deniers, recorded in Sijjīn, with the bliss of the righteous in ‘Illiyyūn, and recalls how the believers were mocked, before they laugh last.

The surah opens with the sky splitting and the earth being leveled on the Last Day, reminding humans that they are toiling towards their Lord. It contrasts those given their record in the right hand with those given it behind the back, wonders at the disbelievers' denial, and promises believers an unending reward.

The surah recalls the people of the trench, who tortured believers for their faith, warns persecutors of Hell and promises believers gardens and the supreme triumph. It stresses God's power and forgiveness, cites the fate of Pharaoh and Thamud, and affirms the Qur'an's glory and preservation.

This Meccan surah swears by the sky and the night comer that every soul has a watcher. It invites man to reflect on his origin as proof that God can resurrect him on the Day secrets are exposed, then affirms the Qur'an as a decisive word and warns that the disbelievers' scheming will fail.

The surah calls for glorifying the Most High Lord, who creates, proportions, decrees and guides, and reassures the Prophet that the Qur'an will be preserved for him. It contrasts the one who purifies himself and remembers God with the wretched who faces the Fire, stressing that the Hereafter is better and more lasting, as the earlier scriptures of Abraham and Moses taught.

The surah describes the Day of Judgment, contrasting humiliated, tormented faces with joyful ones in a lofty garden. It then calls people to reflect on the creation of the camel, sky, mountains and earth, tells the Prophet to remind without compelling, and ends by stating that all return to God for reckoning.

The surah opens with oaths by the dawn and the ten nights, then recalls the destruction of ʿĀd, Thamūd and Pharaoh, who transgressed and spread corruption. It shows how people misread both ease and hardship as tests, rebukes neglect of orphans and the poor and love of wealth, describes the Day of Judgment, and ends by calling the tranquil soul into Paradise.

A Meccan surah that swears by Makkah, and by parent and child, that humans are created into hardship. It rebukes arrogant pride in wealth and the false belief of being unseen, recalls God's gifts and guidance, defines the steep path as freeing slaves, feeding orphans and the needy, faith, patience and compassion, and contrasts the people of the Right and Left.

The surah swears by the sun, moon, day, night, sky, earth and the soul, then states that God inspired the soul with awareness of wrongdoing and righteousness: whoever purifies it succeeds, whoever corrupts it fails. It gives the example of Thamūd, who rejected their prophet, killed the she-camel and were destroyed.

The surah swears by night, day and the creation of male and female that people's efforts differ. Whoever gives, fears God and believes in the best reward is eased toward ease; the miser who denies is eased toward hardship, and wealth cannot save him. It warns of the Fire and promises the most righteous contentment.

A Meccan surah reassuring the Prophet that his Lord has neither forsaken nor despised him, that the Hereafter will be better, and that he will be given until he is pleased. It recalls God's favors in orphanhood, need and guidance, and urges kindness to orphans and beggars and gratitude for God's blessings.

This Meccan surah consoles the Prophet ﷺ in a time of hardship, recalling God's favors: a reassured heart, a lifted burden, and raised renown. It affirms that ease accompanies hardship, then urges him, once free of a task, to strive in worship and turn to his Lord alone.

The surah swears by the fig, the olive, Mount Sinai and the secure city that humans were created in the best form, yet may sink to the lowest of the low, except believers who do good and will receive an unending reward. It closes by questioning denial of the Judgment and affirming God's perfect justice.

The surah opens with the first verses revealed, commanding the Prophet to read in the name of the Lord who created and taught by the pen. It warns against man's arrogance when he deems himself self-sufficient, reminds him of the return to God, threatens one who forbids a servant from praying, and ends with a call to prostrate and draw near.

This surah speaks of the Night of Decree, in which the Qur'an was sent down, and stresses its greatness: it is better than a thousand months. The angels and the Spirit descend by God's permission with every decree, and the night is peace until dawn.

The surah speaks of a messenger sent with clear proof and purified pages to the People of the Book and the polytheists. It notes that divisions arose only after that proof, though they were commanded to worship God sincerely, pray and give zakah, and it contrasts the fate of disbelievers with the reward of the righteous believers.

The surah describes the violent quaking of the earth on the Last Day, as it throws out its burdens and bears witness to what happened upon it by God's inspiration. People come forward in groups to be shown their deeds, and even an atom's weight of good or evil will be seen.

The surah swears by war horses charging at dawn amid clouds of dust, to affirm that man is ungrateful to his Lord, a witness against himself, and intensely fond of wealth. It closes by recalling the Resurrection, when graves are overturned and hearts' secrets revealed, and God is fully aware of all.

The surah describes the terrors of the Day of Judgment, when people will be like scattered moths and mountains like carded wool. It then declares each person's fate by the weighing of deeds: a pleasant life for those whose scales are heavy, and the abyss, a blazing fire, for those whose scales are light.

This surah warns that rivalry over wealth and status distracts people until they reach their graves. It stresses that the truth will become certain to them, mentions the sight of the Blazing Fire, and ends by saying everyone will be asked on Judgment Day about the blessings they enjoyed.

A short Meccan surah that swears by time to declare that humankind is in loss. Only those who combine four qualities are spared: faith, righteous deeds, urging one another to the truth, and urging one another to patience.

This Meccan surah warns against backbiting and slander, and against hoarding wealth in the belief that it brings immortality. It declares the fate of such people: the Crushing Fire, Allah's kindled Fire, which reaches the hearts and is closed down upon them with towering columns.

This short surah recalls the destruction of the people of the Elephant, an army that came to demolish the Kaaba in Mecca before the Prophet's birth. God sent flocks of birds pelting them with baked clay stones, leaving them like chewed chaff. It reminds readers of God's power and His protection of His House.

The surah reminds the Quraysh of God's favors: the security of their winter and summer trading journeys, granted through the protection of the Sacred House. It calls them to worship the Lord of this House alone, who fed them against hunger and secured them against fear.

The surah shows that denying the Recompense is revealed in conduct: harshness toward the orphan and neglect of the needy. It warns those who pray heedlessly and for show, and who withhold small kindnesses, teaching that true worship joins sincerity with compassion.

The shortest surah of the Qur'an announces to the Prophet a great gift from God, al-Kawthar, meaning abundant good. It calls him to give thanks through prayer and sacrifice for God alone. It is traditionally read as a reply to those who mocked him for lacking male offspring: the one truly cut off is his enemy.

This short surah declares a complete separation between the worship of God alone and the worship of anything else. Revealed in Mecca, it is known as a reply to the Quraysh's proposal of a religious compromise, and it closes with the principle: "You have your religion and I have mine."

This surah announces Allah's help, the conquest and people entering Islam in multitudes, then bids the Prophet glorify and praise his Lord and seek forgiveness. Revealed near the end of his mission, it is often understood as a sign that his task was nearing completion.

This Meccan surah announces the ruin of Abu Lahab, the Prophet's uncle, who opposed and harmed him from the start of his preaching; neither his wealth nor his gains will help him. It adds that his wife will share his punishment in a flaming fire, showing the end of hostility to the truth.

A short Meccan surah that distills pure monotheism: God is One, the Eternal Refuge to whom all turn, without parent or child, and without equal. Tradition says it was revealed in response to people who asked the Prophet ﷺ to describe his Lord.

This short surah teaches the believer to seek refuge with the Lord of the daybreak from the harm of creation, the darkness of night, those who practise sorcery by blowing on knots, and the envier. Tradition links it to an episode of sorcery against the Prophet; with the next surah it forms the two surahs of refuge.

The surah instructs the reader to seek refuge with the Lord, Sovereign and God of mankind from the harm of the lurking whisperer, who casts doubts into hearts, whether from jinn or people. Short and closing the Qur'an, it is often recited with the previous surah for protection.
